title: The basics are enough
hook: a man asks if the obligations alone take him to the garden, and is told yes (Nawawi 22, Jabir)
tomorrow: how can washing your hands be half of faith?

segments.voice: Yesterday: say it, then stand, one sentence for life. Today, a man asks whether standing on the basics alone will be enough.

The page loads. Not in, not out: deferred. And a to-do list starts growing on its own: four more clubs, a new essay, a volunteer project by January. Long before any portal, a man came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with the opposite plan. If I pray the prescribed prayers, fast Ramadan, treat the lawful as lawful and the forbidden as forbidden, and add nothing to that, will I enter the Garden? The answer was yes. And the man swore: by Allah, I won't add a thing.
screen: `NOT IN, NOT OUT.` → `THE LIST STARTS GROWING.` → `WILL THE BASICS BE ENOUGH?` → `I WON'T ADD A THING.`

segments.voice: That's al-Nawawi's twenty-second hadith, from Sahih Muslim, told by Jabir. Here's the cliffhanger answered: nobody scolds him. He promises the obligations and nothing extra, and in this telling he isn't told to aim higher. The story ends there. No follow-up, no but surely you'll want more. Just yes. So why would a collection of foundations include a man setting his bar at the floor? Because the floor holds up the house. The obligations aren't a warm-up before the real religion. They're its load-bearing part: the prayer kept on time, the fast kept whole, the lawful and the forbidden treated as what they are. Done well, that's a life. Keeping a prayer on time, every day, can take more discipline than one big night of extra worship. And look at his list again. It isn't only rituals. 'The forbidden as forbidden' is on it: what you won't touch, which can take the most effort of all. Extras still matter in the tradition; other hadith praise voluntary worship. But this one is for the person staring at a growing list, convinced nothing counts unless it's more. Something to tell a friend tonight: the man swore he'd add nothing, and the yes still stood. The basics, done well.
screen: `NOBODY SCOLDS HIM.` · `THE FLOOR HOLDS UP THE HOUSE.` · `WHAT YOU WON'T TOUCH COUNTS TOO.` · `EXTRAS MATTER. THIS IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `THE BASICS, DONE WELL.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the plain, required things you already do most days, whatever they are for you: the prayer you keep, the promise you don't break, the line you won't cross. Let each finger land slowly. When you run out, rest your hands, and let the count stand as it is. A short count can still be a real one.
The basics are enough: the man's question, and the Prophet's yes. The floor is what holds the house up, even when nobody looks at it.
For the road: the basics, done well, not the minimum by accident but the foundation on purpose. Hadith twenty-two, counted.

screen: `DAY 1450 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY · 22 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: HOW CAN WASHING YOUR HANDS BE HALF OF FAITH?`

howItsDone: Muslim teachers use this hadith to reassure new and returning Muslims that the obligations, the five daily prayers, the Ramadan fast and keeping the halal and haram, are the core, with voluntary acts built on top.

chat.meaning: The man kept the obligations, added nothing, and heard yes. The basics, done well, are a foundation, not a fallback.

Jabir.meaning: Jabir ibn Abdullah, the companion who tells it

Ramadan.meaning: the month of fasting in the Islamic calendar

Garden.meaning: paradise, in the Qur'an's own word for it

Sahih Muslim.meaning: a major hadith collection, compiled by Imam Muslim

al-Nawawi.meaning: the scholar from Syria who gathered the Forty

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 22; Sahih Muslim 15 (Jabir ibn Abdullah)
